outline.chapter_title: Factual Narrative and Procedural Path to the Tenth Circuit
outline.description: This chapter introduces the petitioners, reconstructs the sequence of events in Colombia, and shows how the case arrived at the court of appeals. It should emphasize the two overlapping factual stories in the record: the family’s political activity for the Colombian Liberal Party and Jimenez’s separate involvement in a property dispute that exposed alleged criminal activity linked to Don Rafa. That dual narrative is essential to understanding the court’s later nexus analysis.
subtopics: The petitioners: Wilson Leonardo Canon Jimenez, Angelica Parada Duarte, and their two sons
Life in Bogota: the family furniture factory, residence, and departure to the United States in December 2022
Political background: membership in the Colombian Liberal Party since 2012 and support for Federico Gutierrez in the 2022 presidential campaign
Initial campaign-related threats: repeated phone calls and the kidnapping and murder of a political colleague
Jimenez’s professional role: provisional law license, law studies, and internship with the Colombian National Prosecutor’s office
The property dispute: representation of a woman seeking rent and possession from her ex-husband
Discovery of Don Rafa’s identity and the alleged criminal uses of the property
Warnings from local law enforcement to avoid involvement with the property
Escalation of threats: the threatening brochure, the gunpoint confrontation at the factory, the later assault on an employee, and the reference to Don Rafa
The school incident involving the younger son and the family’s temporary move to Jimenez’s mother’s home in the Bogota countryside
Limited police contact before departure and the family’s decision to leave Colombia
Removal proceedings in the United States: Notices to Appear, concessions of removability, asylum and withholding applications, and derivative treatment of the children
The IJ’s decision, the BIA’s affirmance, and the narrowing of issues on petition for review

outline.chapter_title: Appellate Posture, Standard of Review, and the Governing Asylum Framework
outline.description: This chapter explains the legal structure within which the Tenth Circuit reviewed the case. It should clarify what the court could review, why the BIA’s fact findings received deference, and what the petitioners had to prove to obtain asylum or withholding of removal. It should also identify which claims or theories were abandoned or not preserved, because those limits shaped the court’s analysis.
subtopics: Jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. § 1252 to review the final order of removal
Review of the BIA’s decision with consultation of the IJ’s fuller reasoning when the BIA adopts the same grounds
The substantial-evidence standard: when factual findings are conclusive unless any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to disagree
Asylum as discretionary relief and the statutory definition of a 'refugee'
The two basic routes to asylum relevance in this case: past persecution and well-founded fear of future persecution
The three elements of past persecution by private actors: qualifying harm, nexus to a protected ground, and persecution by forces the government is unable or unwilling to control
The significance of a past-persecution showing: rebuttable presumption of a well-founded fear
The relationship between asylum and withholding of removal, including withholding’s higher burden
Claims not pursued on appeal: CAT protection and the due process/right-to-counsel argument
The court’s treatment of protected grounds: political opinion argued, particular social group effectively undeveloped and not meaningfully briefed

outline.chapter_title: Why the Court Found No Past Persecution
outline.description: This chapter focuses on the court’s conclusion that the petitioners’ experiences, even viewed cumulatively, did not rise to the level of persecution under Tenth Circuit precedent. It should explain the court’s understanding of persecution, its treatment of threats, and its reasoning about emotional and psychological harm in the absence of significant physical injury.
subtopics: Persecution as an undefined statutory term filled in by case law
The Tenth Circuit’s formulation: persecution requires offensive infliction of suffering or harm and more than mere restrictions or threats
The cumulative-effects principle: incidents must be considered together rather than in isolation
The evidentiary importance of the petitioners’ concession that they suffered no lasting physical harm
Why threats alone generally do not amount to persecution in this circuit
The court’s treatment of psychological and emotional effects, including Duarte’s sleep problems and the child’s panic and stress
The distinction between serious fear and legally sufficient persecution
Use of precedent to benchmark severity, including cases involving arrest, detention, robberies, machete threats, or repeated threatening calls
How the substantial-evidence standard framed the inquiry: not whether persecution could be found, but whether the BIA was compelled to find it
The chapter’s bottom line: substantial evidence supported the BIA’s conclusion that the aggregate harm fell short of past persecution

outline.chapter_title: Nexus to a Protected Ground: Political Opinion Versus Retaliation for the Don Rafa Conflict
outline.description: This chapter explains the core causation dispute in the case. The petitioners framed their mistreatment as persecution on account of political opinion, but the court concluded that the record supported a different motive: retaliation for Jimenez’s involvement with Don Rafa’s property and his perceived role as a 'snitch' connected to law enforcement. This chapter should show how the court moved from the facts to the statutory 'one central reason' standard.
subtopics: The protected-ground issue preserved for review: political opinion rather than a developed particular social group theory
The statutory nexus requirement that a protected ground be 'at least one central reason' for the harm
The meaning of 'central reason': not incidental, tangential, superficial, subordinate, or minor
Mixed-motive persecution doctrine and why multiple motives do not defeat a claim if a protected ground remains central
The court’s distinction between early campaign-related threats and later escalated threats tied to the property dispute
The lack of evidence that Don Rafa was responsible for the initial politically themed threatening calls
Why timing mattered: serious threats intensified only after Jimenez confronted the tenant and investigated the property
The attackers’ own words: references to Jimenez as a 'snitch,' his prosecutor’s office connection, and responsibility for searches and seizures
The significance of the threat to factory employees that the order came from Don Rafa
The court’s conclusion that the predominant motive was protection of Don Rafa’s criminal operation, revenue, and security
Why the court characterized any political motive as merely tangential or subordinate
The role of appellate deference: the court would not reweigh competing inferences where substantial evidence supported the agency’s view

outline.chapter_title: Future Persecution, Government Protection, Internal Relocation, and Final Disposition
outline.description: This chapter brings together the remaining elements of the asylum claim and the court’s final disposition. It explains why the petitioners could not show the Colombian government was unable or unwilling to protect them, why the record supported safe internal relocation, and why failure on the asylum claim necessarily defeated withholding of removal.
subtopics: Why the court turned to future persecution even after rejecting past persecution
The unable-or-unwilling requirement in private-actor cases and its focus on governmental response
The importance of notice to the government and the usual relevance of reporting persecution to police or other authorities
The limited efforts to seek protection in this case: conversations with two police officers rather than formal reporting or broader institutional contact
Why isolated comments from individual officers did not establish the position or incapacity of the Colombian state
The court’s emphasis that Jimenez and his father had government or law-enforcement connections yet did not pursue wider channels of protection
The petitioners’ futility-and-danger argument based on alleged alignment between persecutors and the Colombian government
Evidence undermining that argument: prior searches and seizures at the property and the government’s existing awareness of criminal activity there
The conclusion that the record did not compel a finding that Colombia was unable or unwilling to protect the family
Internal relocation doctrine, including the regulatory idea that persecution may be avoidable by moving elsewhere in the country

Why the court found relocation reasonable here: the family stayed safely with Jimenez’s mother in the countryside, relatives remained unharmed in Colombia, and the threats were framed as demands to leave the neighborhood rather than the country
The petitioners’ contrary relocation arguments about economics, administration, and national political ties, and why the court viewed them as insufficiently supported
The final holding: petition for review denied
The withholding consequence: because the petitioners failed to satisfy asylum’s lower standard, they necessarily failed to satisfy the higher standard for withholding of removal

Case significance: the decision illustrates the difficulty of proving asylum where harm comes from private criminals, reporting to the state is limited, and the record supports a nonpolitical motive for threats
